strengths: Addresses an underexplored direction: training-free spatial acceleration for diffusion transformers. While temporal (caching) acceleration is crowded, the spatial axis has essentially only Bottleneck Sampling as prior art, and this paper identifies and clearly characterizes two failure modes (aliasing at edges, noise-timestep mismatch) that arise from latent upsampling during denoising.

The noise-timestep rescheduling (NT-DM) component is technically sound and non-trivial: the derivation that upsampled latents leave the rectified-flow trajectory (non-isotropic covariance from the upsampling matrix Σ), and the closed-form solution for correlated noise injection and rescheduled timesteps (Eq. 5–6, Appendix A.1), is convincing. Framing timestep selection as Jensen-Shannon divergence minimization against the original model's timestep distribution is a principled, training-free solution.

Empirical results are strong and broad: up to 7× speedup on FLUX.1-dev and 3× on SD3 with FID/NIQE/CLIP-IQA/GenEval/T2I-CompBench consistently better than both ToCa and Bottleneck Sampling at matched budgets, plus demonstrated complementarity with caching (4.13×→5.00×, 7.02×→7.94×).

Good ablation coverage: the NT-DM hyperparameter ablation (Tab. 4), upsampling-ratio trade-off (Fig. 6), upsampling-timing sensitivity (Fig. S1), caching integration details, and large sets of uncurated results (Figs. S8–S11) mitigate cherry-picking concerns. Baseline configurations are documented in sufficient detail to reproduce (Appendix B.2, B.5).

The paper is honest about scope: limitations state NT-DM is tailored to flow matching and unverified for score/DDIM-style models, and the extra VAE decode cost is quantified (0.08%/0.71% of total FLOPs).
weaknesses: The central empirical claim needs a caveat: comparing against simple step reduction at matched compute, FLUX(12) and FLUX(7) achieve FID of 28.42 and 27.33 respectively, versus RALU's 28.30 and 28.68 (Tab. 1). On pure image fidelity, RALU is roughly at parity with (at 7×, slightly worse than) just using fewer steps. RALU's advantage at matched latency is mainly in text alignment (T2I-Comp 0.566 vs 0.532; GenEval 0.646 vs 0.585 at 7×) and NIQE. The paper should foreground this comparison rather than only comparing against acceleration methods, and better articulate when spatial acceleration is preferable to simply lowering step counts.

Generalization is limited: only 2× region granularity is studied (a single halving of latent resolution), only two flow-matching T2I models are evaluated, and neither video DiTs nor DDPM-style models are covered despite the introduction's broad framing. The stage boundaries (e1, e2), upsampling ratio, and c appear dataset/model-specific and determined by numerical search; sensitivity to these hyperparameters is underexplored beyond Tab. 4.

Some design choices are heuristic and under-justified: edge-region identification via VAE decoding the Tweedie estimate and applying Canny edge detection to select top-k patches is reasonable but ad hoc; no comparison against alternative saliency/edge criteria (e.g., latent-gradient or attention-based selection) is provided, leaving unclear whether Canny specifically matters.

Novelty is moderate: the correlated-noise injection is explicitly acknowledged as inspired by the training-based Pyramidal Flow Matching [21], and the three-stage high-low-high structure closely mirrors Bottleneck Sampling [46]; the contribution is largely the training-free adaptation plus distribution matching. This is a worthwhile but incremental contribution.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places: the FID reference set and number of samples used for the T2I evaluations are not specified, no code release is mentioned, and several evaluated configurations depend on per-model searched values (Tab. S1). Minor presentation issues further reduce polish (e.g., Table 4 lists GenEval with a '↓' though higher is better; 'preserve noise-related artifacts' should read 'prevent'; incomplete parentheses in the Fig. 3 caption/Eq. 8 reference).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored direction (training-free spatial acceleration for DiTs) and clearly motivates the two failure modes (aliasing and noise-timestep mismatch) that arise from mixed-resolution sampling.

The noise-timestep rescheduling (NT-DM) is derived carefully: the correlated-noise injection in Eq. (4)-(6) and the closed-form solution in Appendix A.1 are technically sound and correctly extend the training-based correlated-noise idea of Pyramidal Flow Matching [21] to a training-free setting, including the validity constraint 0 <= c <= 1/4.

Quantitative evidence is fairly comprehensive: five metrics (FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, T2I-CompBench, GenEval) across two strong models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3), comparisons against both temporal (ToCa, RAS) and spatial (Bottleneck Sampling) baselines, a caching-integration experiment showing complementary gains (4.13x -> 5.00x, 7.02x -> 7.94x), an ablation of the NT-DM parameters, an upsampling-ratio study, and uncurated qualitative results to mitigate cherry-picking concerns.

At matched FLOPs, RALU consistently beats the closest training-free baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) on image quality (e.g., FID 28.30 vs 34.48 at 4x on FLUX; 28.68 vs 38.16 at 7x), supporting the central claim.

Limitations and broader impact are explicitly discussed, and implementation details (baseline configurations, FLOPs of the VAE-decoder edge-detection overhead, caching setup) are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the overall framework closely mirrors Bottleneck Sampling [46] (three-stage high-low-high resolution training-free sampling), and the noise-injection mechanism is explicitly adapted from Pyramidal Flow Matching [21]. The main new ingredients are (a) edge-region-selective upsampling via Canny edge detection plus top-k patch selection, which is a fairly heuristic patch-level design choice, and (b) a JSD-based timestep schedule search solved by numerical search. The combination is sensible but incremental.

The edge-selection stage is under-justified and somewhat crude: operating at the patch level with nearest-neighbor upsampling on top-k Canny-dense patches may cause seams between upsampled and non-upsampled regions; the paper asserts consistency is ensured in Stage 3 but provides no quantitative or focused visual analysis of boundary seams, nor a comparison against alternative saliency/edge criteria.

Some evaluation aspects are weak: human perceptual evaluation is absent, and NIQE/CLIP-IQA are noisy proxies for generation quality; the reported wins on FID alone would strengthen confidence, but the user study-level evidence for the 'visually faithful' claim is limited to curated and uncurated figure montages.

Presentation and consistency issues reduce confidence: Table 4 marks GenEval with a down arrow although higher is better (and the ablation differences are small, within noise for a single-seed run of 2,212 GenEval images); there are textual errors such as 'preserve noise-related artifacts' (should be 'prevent') and malformed equation references in the Fig. 3 caption ('(Eq. (8) and the modified distribution (Eq. (9)'). The single-fixed-seed protocol across metrics is stated but statistical variance is not reported.

Generalization is narrow: NT-DM is derived specifically for rectified-flow/flow-matching models and the method is validated only on FLUX.1-dev and SD3 (Medium); no DiT-class model (e.g., PixArt, HunyuanDiT) or video model is tested, which limits the claimed breadth of the framework despite the Limitations section acknowledging this.

The headline 7.0x speedup is partly an artifact of comparison framing: the reference is the 50-step baseline, while RALU at 7x uses only 7 total steps with rescheduling; the more meaningful comparison—RALU vs. reduced-step FLUX at similar FLOPs—shows quality gains but a much smaller effective speedup, and this should be stated more transparently.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored direction: training-free spatial (resolution) acceleration for diffusion transformers, complementing the well-studied temporal caching literature. The paper correctly identifies latent upsampling as the core obstacle.

The problem analysis is principled rather than heuristic. Section 3 decomposes the failure modes into aliasing artifacts (localized at edges) and noise-timestep mismatch artifacts (global), each supported by visual evidence (Figs. 2 and 4) and by a temporal sensitivity study in §C.1.

The NT-DM component has a clean mathematical derivation: the authors show why the upsampled latent leaves the rectified-flow trajectory (Eqs. 2-4, Σ not proportional to identity), derive the correlated-noise correction with Σ' = I − cΣ (Appendix A.1), and cast timestep rescheduling as JSD minimization between the target and actual timestep distributions (Eqs. 7-9). This is a more principled treatment than the heuristic rescheduling of Bottleneck Sampling.

Quantitative results are broad and consistent: five metrics (FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, T2I-CompBench, GenEval) on two flow-matching DiTs (FLUX.1-dev, SD3) at multiple operating points (4×/7× and 2×/3×), with RALU outperforming both ToCa and Bottleneck Sampling at matched compute, and degrading gracefully at aggressive 7× acceleration where ToCa collapses (FID 159.50 vs 28.68).

Demonstrated complementarity with caching (5.00× and 7.94× combined speedups in Table 3) strengthens the practical value, and the overhead of the VAE/Canny edge-selection step is properly accounted for (§B.6, <1% of FLOPs).

Reproducibility support is above average: baseline configurations are fully specified (§B.2), NT-DM hyperparameters are reported (Table S1), the optimization is a numerical search (not per-prompt tuning), and uncurated 96-prompt CC12M generations (Figs. S8-S11) mitigate cherry-picking concerns.
weaknesses: The comparison against simply reducing inference steps weakens the value proposition at some operating points. In Table 1, FLUX.1-dev (12 steps) achieves FID 28.42 / NIQE 7.49 at latency 5.75s, essentially matching RALU (FID 28.30, NIQE 6.54, latency 5.55s), and RALU actually scores lower on T2I-CompBench (0.549 vs 0.565). At 7×, RALU's FID (28.68) is worse than the naive 7-step baseline (27.33), though it wins on alignment metrics. The paper should more directly articulate what spatial acceleration adds over trivial step reduction, since latency is comparable.

Novelty is moderate and partly derivative: the correlated-noise injection is explicitly acknowledged as inspired by the training-based Pyramidal Flow Matching [21], and the three-stage low-high-resolution skeleton closely follows Bottleneck Sampling [46]. The contribution is a training-free refinement of these ideas (edge-selective early upsampling + distribution-matched rescheduling) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation is limited to T2I generation on two flow-matching models. The authors honestly state in the Limitations section that NT-DM is flow-matching-specific and unverified for score-based/DDIM diffusion, other architectures, video, or 3D/audio modalities. For a CVPR audience, at least one additional domain (e.g., video DiT) would materially strengthen generalization claims.

No human evaluation or user study is provided; the quality claims rest entirely on automatic metrics, some of which (FID at few-sample regimes, CLIP-IQA) have known limitations. The FID reference set / prompt distribution used for FID computation is not clearly specified in the main text.

Several design choices are fixed by search or hand-tuning rather than justified: the number of steps per stage (Table S1), the top-k upsampling ratio (only a coarse 0.1/0.3/0.5 trade-off study in Fig. 6), and the caching ratio 0.4. Sensitivity analysis of c is limited to a ±20% perturbation in Table 4; the interaction between NT-DM parameters and different prompt/image statistics is not explored.
No code release is mentioned, which limits immediate reproducibility of the numerical-search components of NT-DM.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored direction: training-free spatial acceleration of DiTs via latent upsampling, complementing the large body of temporal acceleration work. The framing as an analysis-driven contribution (Sec. 3 identifying aliasing artifacts from late upsampling and distribution-mismatching artifacts from noise/timestep skew) is convincing and each claim is supported by controlled experiments (Fig. 2b: upsampling timestep vs. edge energy/artifact ratio over 100 images; Fig. 3b: JSD vs. ImageReward).

The proposed NT-Matching is technically principled rather than heuristic: the correlated-noise injection is derived by matching the upsampled latent distribution back onto the flow trajectory (Eqs. 4-7, full derivation in Appendix A), and the timestep distribution matching is formulated as an analytic JSD minimization over truncated flow-matching PDFs (Eqs. 8-10). This gives the method a solid theoretical grounding unusual for training-free acceleration papers.

The mixed-resolution design (early upsampling of only the top-r edge patches identified via Tweedie estimate + VAE decode + Canny, late upsampling of the rest) is a sensible resolution of the speed/artifact trade-off, and the paper transparently reports that the adaptive-ratio alternative and latent-space edge detection were tested and did not help (Tabs. S3, S4).

Experiments are broad and reasonably fair: two strong DiT backbones (FLUX.1-dev, SD3), five competitive temporal baselines plus the only prior training-free spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling), multiple complementary metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval), latency measured on both A100 and A6000 with VRAM reported (Tab. S2), and ablations on upsampling ratio, NT-Matching JSD (Tab. 3), and upsampler choice (Tab. S5).

The complementary integrations are valuable and well demonstrated: RALU + temporal caching/forecasting (up to 9.03x) and RALU on timestep-distilled models (15.91x on FLUX.1-schnell), with quantitative and uncurated qualitative evidence (Figs. S10-S13, 96 random CC12M prompts) that reduces cherry-picking concerns.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited: only two text-to-image DiT backbones, both flow-matching based, and the authors themselves acknowledge in Sec. D that NT-Matching is flow-matching specific and untested on other backbones (e.g., DDPM-based DiTs, U-Nets, video models). This constrains the demonstrated generality of the core contribution.

No FID or human evaluation is reported. The quality assessment relies entirely on proxy metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, GenEval, T2I-CompBench); given the paper's central claim is artifact suppression, FID on a standard benchmark or a small user study would substantially strengthen the case.

The empirical claims around JSD are slightly inconsistent: Fig. 3b states mismatching artifacts essentially vanish at JSD < 0.03, yet the optimized SD3-2x configuration in Tab. S1 has JSD = 0.0586, above that threshold, without discussion. Additionally, NT-Matching parameters {hk, c} are found by per-model, per-speedup numerical search, raising questions about tuning burden and sensitivity that are only partially addressed by Tab. 3.

Mixed-resolution denoising mechanics are under-analyzed: how self-attention and cross-attention behave when tokens of different resolutions are concatenated is acknowledged in Sec. 6 as an open question rather than investigated. The computational accounting for the VAE decode + Canny step is reported, which helps, but the per-stage cost breakdown of the three-stage pipeline itself is not given.

The only direct spatial-acceleration baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) is an arXiv preprint, so the comparative evidence for the spatial setting rests on a single non-peer-reviewed competitor; comparisons against reduced-NFE and temporal baselines are useful but not equivalent settings. Reported latency gains at matched FLOPs (e.g., 3.75s vs. 3.79s for FLUX 7x) are also modest, meaning the practical advantage is mainly quality at equal cost rather than additional speed.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and empirically characterizes two distinct failure modes of naïve latent upsampling in flow-matching DiTs (aliasing from late upsampling in edge regions, and trajectory/timestep distribution mismatch after noise injection), supported by controlled experiments (Figs. 2b, 3b) with 100-image averages rather than anecdotes.

The proposed remedy is well-motivated and training-free: mixed-resolution sampling that upsamples only artifact-prone edge patches early, plus an analytically derived correlated-noise injection and JSD-minimizing timestep schedule (NT-Matching). The derivation in Appendix A is transparent, including the constraint 0 ≤ c ≤ 1/4 for 2× nearest-neighbor upsampling.

Evaluation breadth is above average for an acceleration paper: two base models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3-Medium), five metrics spanning quality and text alignment, multiple speedup settings, integration with temporal caching methods (Δ-DiT, ToCa, TaylorSeer) and timestep-distilled models (FLUX.1-schnell, SD3.5L-Turbo), latency benchmarks on two GPU architectures, and uncurated qualitative results (Figs. S10–S13) to reduce cherry-picking concerns.

Ablations cover the key design choices: edge detection method (Tab. S3), fixed vs. adaptive upsampling ratio (Tab. S4), upsampler choice (Tab. S5), upsampling ratio trade-off (Fig. 8), and JSD level for NT-Matching (Tab. 3). The honest reporting that adaptive ratio does not help and that nearest-neighbor is chosen partly for tractable covariance computation is appreciated.
weaknesses: The 'artifact ratio' metric underpinning the central claims (Figs. 2b, 3b, 7) appears to be a self-defined, judgment-based measure (proportion of images with 'visible aliasing' / 'mismatching artifacts'). The annotation protocol, inter-rater agreement, and number of human raters are not described, so the quantitative artifact comparisons against Bottleneck Sampling are hard to verify or reproduce.

The two contributions are somewhat incremental when placed against prior work: early upsampling of coarse content and correlated noise injection with schedule re-shifting are closely related to mechanisms in Pyramidal Flow [24], Relay Diffusion [54], and Bottleneck Sampling [55] (which the appendix itself credits with noise re-introduction and scheduler re-shifting). The delta over these baselines is primarily the region-adaptive (edge-only) upsampling and the training-free JSD-based schedule matching, and the paper could articulate this boundary more sharply.

The headline claims (7.0× on FLUX, 3.0× on SD3) are FLOPs-based; the actually measured latency speedups in Table 1 are more modest (5.53× and 3.02×), and the 15.9× figure requires combining with a distilled model, which is a different (training-based) acceleration axis. The abstract's framing slightly overstates the practical gains.

Comparisons in Table 1 are not perfectly controlled: baselines appear at somewhat different TFLOPs/speedup operating points (e.g., FLUX 5× block mixes 3.87×–5.53×), and no variance or significance testing is reported for any of the quantitative metrics, so small advantages (e.g., RALU 0.999 vs. Bottleneck 0.792 ImageReward is large, but GenEval 0.652 vs. 0.687 favors the baseline) are hard to weigh.

The method involves several hyperparameters (stage boundaries [N1,N2,N3], e = [e1,e2,e3], top-r ratio, and the numerically searched {hk}, c) that appear tuned per model and per speedup setting (Tab. S1). Sensitivity of the final result to these choices, and the cost of re-tuning for a new model, are not discussed; this partially weakens the 'training-free, plug-and-play' positioning.

Generality is limited and acknowledged only late: NT-Matching is tailored to flow-matching DiTs, and all experiments use only two T2I models. No results on video DiTs or non-flow backbones, so applicability beyond the tested setting remains unverified.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and underexplored problem—training-free spatial acceleration for DiTs—and provides a well-designed empirical study of two distinct artifact sources (aliasing from late upsampling, and distribution/timestep mismatching after upsampling), each supported by quantitative experiments (Fig. 2: edge energy and artifact ratio vs. upsampling timestep; Fig. 3: ImageReward and artifact ratio vs. JSD with statistical significance noted).

The proposed RALU is a clean, training-free solution: mixed-resolution upsampling restricted to artifact-prone edge regions (identified via Tweedie's estimate + VAE decode + Canny) and an NT-Matching scheme with a principled derivation (Appendix A) that analytically matches the post-upsampling distribution and minimizes JSD of the timestep distribution. The components map directly onto the diagnosed failure modes.

Results are convincing and thorough: consistent gains over the only direct spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) and strong temporal baselines (∆-DiT, ToCa, TeaCache, TaylorSeer, RAS) on both FLUX.1-dev and SD3 across 2×–7× settings and five evaluation metrics (Tab. 1); up to 7.02× speedup at near-baseline quality, and demonstrated composability with temporal accelerators (up to 9.03×) and distilled models (15.91×) with only modest metric degradation (Tab. 2).

Reproducibility is strong: the appendix provides complete derivations, determined NT-Matching parameters (Tab. S1), full baseline configurations, hardware/latency/memory details on two GPUs (Tab. S2), and additional ablations (edge detection method, fixed vs. adaptive ratio, upsampler choice), plus uncurated qualitative results.

The ablation studies justify design choices quantitatively (e.g., Tab. S3–S5 show VAE+Canny beats a latent gradient kernel at <1% FLOPs overhead, fixed-ratio beats adaptive with zero FLOPs variance, nearest-neighbor upsampling works best under SNR matching), and the limitations of NT-Matching (flow-matching-specific) are honestly stated.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two image-generation models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3 Medium); no video DiT, no U-Net backbone, and no non-flow-matching DiT is tested, so the generality of the framework—and especially NT-Matching, which is explicitly tailored to flow matching—remains unverified outside this narrow family.

Several core settings are empirical and heuristic rather than principled: the aliasing threshold (t_up ≤ 0.3), the 2× upsampling factor only, and the top-r ratio (0.2–0.3) are justified by observation rather than theory; the JSD threshold (0.03) for artifact-free operation appears derived from a single empirical plot averaged over 100 images.

The numerical search for {h_k}, c adds per-configuration hyperparameters that must be re-tuned for each model/speedup combination (Tab. S1 shows four distinct settings), which somewhat weakens the 'training-free, plug-and-play' narrative; no sensitivity analysis of this search is provided.

The mechanism by which the DiT processes mixed-resolution token sets (self-attention across H/2 and H patches) is acknowledged as not understood (Sec. 6), so the method relies on empirical robustness of DiTs to heterogeneous inputs rather than a mechanistic explanation; this leaves open questions about failure cases or model families where it might break.

Comparisons with temporal baselines, while configurations are documented, compare methods under settings chosen by the authors (e.g., specific N, W, δ values); the fairness of these comparisons is plausible but the baselines could conceivably be tuned differently, and latency advantages of RALU over e.g. TeaCache at 7× are modest (3.75s vs. 4.21s).

Edge-region selection depends on a Tweedie estimate decoded through the VAE early in denoising, when the clean-image estimate may be unreliable; the paper does not analyze how edge-map quality or mis-selection affects final results beyond the aggregate metrics.
